The nonnegative scaled squared-norm sum has each exact squared input multiplied by at most $r+2$ factors $1+\delta$, $|\delta|\le u$: two from scaling and at most $r$ from squaring and subsequent additions. Thus the computed norm divided by $N$ lies between $(1-u)^{r/2+3}$ and $(1+u)^{r/2+3}$ after square root and rescaling. For exponent $p\ge1$, convexity of $t^p$ on $t>0$ gives $1-(1-u)^p\le(1+u)^p-1$. Hence $|\widehat\alpha-\alpha_0|\le e_rN$. Only the first stored coordinate can differ from $v_0$, and subtraction gives $\|v-v_0\|_2\le(e_r+u(2+e_r))N=d_rN$. Success gives nonzero stored $v$.

source_anchors.claim: Fix an output coordinate $j$ of $\widehat\lambda$ and put $q_i=B_{ij}c_i$. By success in [F4] and the relative bound in [F5], $p_i=q_i(1+\alpha_i)$ with $|\alpha_i|\le u$; exact-zero products have $\alpha_i=0$. For each addition $i=2,\ldots,n$, write $s_i=(s_{i-1}+p_i)(1+\beta_i)$ with $|\beta_i|\le u$, taking $\beta_i=0$ when the exact sum is zero. Expanding gives $\widehat\lambda_j=s_n=\sum_{i=1}^n q_i(1+\alpha_i)\prod_{k=\max(2,i)}^n(1+\beta_k)$, with an empty product interpreted as $1$. Each coefficient has at most $n$ factors: for $i=1$ it has one product factor and $n-1$ addition factors, while for $i\ge2$ it has one product factor and $n-i+1$ addition factors. Thus [F6], $nu<1$, and monotonicity of $ku/(1-ku)$ imply that each coefficient differs from $1$ by at most $\gamma_n$. Hence $|\widehat\lambda_j-(B^Tc)_j|\le\gamma_n\sum_i|B_{ij}||c_i|$. Stacking these bounds and applying $\||B|^T|c|\|_2\le\|B\|_F\|c\|_2$ gives $\|\widehat\lambda-B^Tc\|_2\le t\|c\|_2$ and then $\|\widehat\lambda\|_2\le(M+t)\|c\|_2$. Each rounded outer-product entry has error at most $u|\widehat\lambda_i\widehat x_j|$, so its Frobenius error is at most $u(M+t)\|\widehat x\|_2\|c\|_2$. Combining these bounds with step 2.1 gives the stated vector and matrix cotangent estimates.

Since $w_j\ge1$, this node's reverse arithmetic work is at most $(c+ar)w_j$. Summing over all nodes gives total arithmetic work at most $(1+c+ar)W$; cotangent-buffer initialization is storage under [A2].

source_anchors.claim: Induct on $N$. For $N=0$, the empty interval has terminal state $x_{a+N}=x_a$ and unchanged cotangent, exactly the returned pair. For $N=1$, the single evaluation returns its exact output state and its local reverse rule returns the exact input cotangent. For $N\ge2$, midpoint replay produces the exact $x_{a+L}$ by [F3]. By induction the right child returns terminal state $x_{a+N}$ and the exact cotangent at that midpoint; the left child returns terminal state $x_{a+L}$ and, after the earlier transitions, the exact cotangent at $x_a$. The parent returns the right child's terminal state and the left child's starting cotangent, so both outputs are correct. Every interval is split into disjoint left and right steps and each base step is recorded and reversed once. Therefore the terminal value and initial cotangent agree with the ordinary reverse sweep.

source_anchors.claim: Fix $n\ge\max\{1,V(x_0)\}$ and set $K_n=\{x\in E:V(x)\le n\}$. This is finite by properness. The set $D_n=\{x+\nu_j:x\in K_n,\ a_j(x)>0,\ 1\le j\le R\}\setminus K_n$ of one-reaction exit states is finite, and $F_n=K_n\cup D_n$ is finite. The rate bound $M_n:=\max_{x\in K_n}\lambda(x)$ is therefore finite. For fixed ordered channel labels $j_1,\ldots,j_m$, the density of event times $0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\le T$ before the first exit is the product of the successive channel rates and exponential no-event factors. Summing over channel labels bounds this density by $M_n^m$, since at each event the sum of active channel rates is at most $M_n$. The ordered simplex has volume $T^m/m!$, so the probability of at least $m$ events before exit by $T$ is at most $(M_nT)^m/m!$, which tends to zero. Thus infinitely many jumps cannot occur in finite time while the process remains in $K_n$.

source_anchors.claim: Let $\mathcal G_t$ be generated by candidate times and marks up to $t$; these sigma-algebras increase with $t$, so [F5] makes them a continuous-time filtration. If $\Lambda=0$, all rates and all counts vanish. Otherwise the thinning realization has a rate-$\Lambda$ candidate process, and [F2] gives the same reaction path law as Gillespie. By [F3], candidates have no ties and their number on $[0,T]$ is finite almost surely. Hence each $N_j$ is adapted, nondecreasing and integer-valued with unit jumps and finite terminal value; also $N_j(T)\le N^*(T)$ and $0\le A_j(T)\le\Lambda T$. The state path is piecewise constant with finitely many jumps. Its left-limit process $X_{s-}$ is a pointwise limit of left-grid processes taking the value $X_{k2^{-n}}$ on $(k2^{-n},(k+1)2^{-n}]$; each is measurable for the generators in [F4]. Thus $a_j(X_{s-})$ is predictable. Because the density is bounded and piecewise constant along the path, for fixed $t$ its time integral is the limit of left-grid Riemann sums of values known by time $t$, so $A_j(t)$ is $\mathcal G_t$-measurable. The integral is continuous and bounded by $\Lambda T$; continuous adapted processes are pointwise limits of their left-grid predictable approximations, so $A_j$ is predictable with finite mean.

source_anchors.claim: By [F1], the evaluation function of $p$ is $\sum_{k=0}^{m}a_kX^k$; zero padding changes this finite sum by zero terms only. For $0\le r\le m$, define the real function $Q_r(X)=\sum_{k=r}^{m}a_k\bigl(\prod_{s=0}^{r-1}(k-s)\bigr)X^{k-r}$, with the empty product equal to $1$; each factor $k-s$ is natural because $k\ge r>s$.

At $r=0$, $Q_0=p=p^{(0)}$ by [F2]. If $r<m$ and $p^{(r)}=Q_r$, termwise differentiation in [F3] kills the $k=r$ constant term and multiplies each term with $k>r$ by its exponent $k-r$; for each $k>r$, the resulting real coefficient is $a_k\bigl(\prod_{s=0}^{r-1}(k-s)\bigr)(k-r)=a_k\prod_{s=0}^{r}(k-s)$. Indeed the finite natural product extends by its last factor, and [F7] carries that natural identity to the product of canonical real images. The new exponent is $(k-r)-1=k-(r+1)$, so the differentiated sum is exactly $Q_{r+1}$. Hence $p^{(r+1)}=Q_{r+1}$.
